title: L5 Corpectomy in a 12-Year-Old Owing to Rosai-Dorfman Disease: A Case Report.
abstract: Background Rosai-Dorfman disease (RDD) is a rare non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically presenting with massive, painless lymphadenopathy or subcutaneous masses. Extranodal involvement, particularly in the spine, is exceedingly rare and poses significant diagnostic and management challenges. Lumbar spinal RDD with vertebral collapse and neurological compromise is almost unheard of in the pediatric population, with no prior reports of surgical intervention requiring L5 corpectomy and circumferential fusion in an adolescent. Case description We present a case of a 12-year-old girl with a 6-month history of worsening lower back pain unresponsive to conservative treatment. Imaging revealed collapse of the L5 vertebral body and a destructive, enhancing lesion encasing the neural elements, leading to severe canal and foraminal stenosis. Computed tomography-guided biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of RDD. A multidisciplinary surgical team implemented a 2-stage circumferential surgical plan. Stage 1 involved posterior decompression and posterior instrumentation from L3 to the pelvis using S2AI screws. A silastic barrier was placed to protect neural elements. Stage 2, performed via an anterior approach with vascular surgery assistance, involved complete corpectomy of L5 and reconstruction with an expandable cage spanning L4 to S1. Postoperative recovery was uneventful, and the patient remained neurologically intact. At 1-year follow-up, the patient demonstrated solid anterior and posterior fusion, maintained spinal alignment, and had returned to full activity. Conclusion This is the first reported case of pediatric RDD requiring an L5 corpectomy with circumferential spinal fusion. The case underscores the importance of early tissue diagnosis, individualized surgical planning, and interdisciplinary collaboration. Recognition of RDD as a potential etiology for pediatric spinal lesions is critical, particularly when imaging mimics malignancy. Our successful outcome supports the use of staged, tailored surgical approaches in managing rare spinal pathologies in children.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of preoperative magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography in delineating biliary anatomy in live liver donors: An ambispective observational study.
abstract: Backgrounds/aims Accurate preoperative delineation of biliary anatomy is essential for living donor liver transplantation (LDLT), as unrecognised variants contribute to biliary complications. This study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) for characterising biliary anatomy in live donors, using intraoperative cholangiography (IOC) as the reference standard. Methods An ambispective observational study included 89 live liver donors (65 retrospective, 24 prospective) at a tertiary LDLT centre. Biliary anatomy was classified on MRCP and IOC using the Huang classification. Variant anatomy (Huang types A2-A5) was defined as the positive test condition and standard anatomy (A1) as the negative condition. Diagnostic performance was assessed using sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values, and Cohen's kappa. Results The cohort comprised 58 females (65.2%) and 31 males (34.8%), with a mean age of 34.34 ± 9.53 years. Huang type A1 was most common on MRCP (65.2%) and IOC (59.6%), while variants (A2-A5) were detected in 34.8% and 40.4%, respectively. Against IOC, MRCP showed 77.78% sensitivity (95% CI, 61.92%-88.28%), 94.34% specificity (95% CI, 84.63%-98.06%), 90.32% positive predictive value (95% CI, 75.10%-96.65%), 86.21% negative predictive value (95% CI, 75.07%-92.84%), and 87.64% overall accuracy, with substantial agreement (κ = 0.737, p < 0.001). Conclusions MRCP is highly specific for preoperative biliary mapping in LDLT donors but has limited sensitivity for variants, supporting routine IOC before ductal transection.

title: From Sudden Cardiac Death Prevention to Performance Optimization: A Conceptual Framework for Cardiovascular Assessment in Elite Athletes.
abstract: Cardiovascular pre-participation evaluation in elite athletes primarily aims to identify cardiovascular conditions associated with sudden cardiac death. Current international recommendations emphasize comprehensive medical history, physical examination, and resting 12-lead electrocardiography (ECG), with additional investigations guided by clini-cal findings and individual risk. However, advances in sports cardiology, cardiovascular imaging, and exercise physiology provide opportunities to integrate cardiovascular risk assessment with physiological performance evaluation. This article proposes a concep-tual, hypothesis-generating framework integrating structural, electrical, and functional cardiovascular assessment in elite athletes. The framework consists of 3 sequential components: comprehensive clinical assessment with resting ECG; transthoracic echo-cardiography for structural evaluation and longitudinal reference; and cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) as an optional complementary investigation. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing may provide information on maximal oxygen uptake, ventilatory thresh-olds, oxygen pulse, ventilatory efficiency, heart rate recovery, and exercise-induced arrhythmias, potentially supporting individualized training prescription and longitudinal physiological monitoring. Cardiac magnetic resonance and coronary computed tomog-raphy angiography (CCTA) may be considered selectively when clinically indicated. A one-time CCTA strategy during an athlete's career is proposed as a research hypothesis requiring prospective assessment of clinical utility and cost-effectiveness. Importantly, CPET and CCTA are not proposed as universal screening requirements. This framework is intended to complement, rather than replace, current evidence-based international recommendations. As the proposed model is based on available literature and expert opinion and has not undergone prospective clinical validation, future multicenter stud-ies are required to determine whether integrated cardiovascular assessment improves risk stratification, athlete safety, clinical decision-making, performance monitoring, and cost-effectiveness.

title: Growth hormone-releasing hormone-secreting giant pheochromocytoma causing acromegaly: a case report with a review of the literature.
abstract: The ectopic secretion of growth hormone (GH) or growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) is responsible for fewer than 1% of acromegaly cases. Furthermore, within this small population, GHRH-secreting pheochromocytomas/paragangliomas (PPGLs) are even rarer. A 57-year-old Japanese woman presented to our hospital for treatment of a large left-sided pheochromocytoma (PCC). A physical examination revealed enlargement of the nose and lips as well as macroglossia, thereby raising the suspicion of acromegaly, which was biochemically confirmed by a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a slightly enlarged pituitary gland but no definitive tumor. A left adrenalectomy was performed after careful dose titration of doxazosin and metyrosine. Postoperative biochemical improvement of GH excess and immunohistochemical analysis of the resected tumor confirmed the diagnosis of GHRH-secreting PCC. Given the possibility that PPGLs produce various ectopic hormones and peptides, thorough physical examinations remain fundamental for the accurate diagnosis and optimal management of patients with these tumors.

title: Multiple classification of childhood and juvenile autism spectrum disorder from ABIDE-II sMRI using BN-GO-CNN.
abstract: Objectives Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) shows heterogeneous neurodevelopmental patterns across childhood, juvenile development, and adulthood, so binary MRI classification may not fully capture age-and sex-related variation. This study proposes a proof-of-concept framework for multiple classification using ABIDE-II T1-weighted structural MRI (sMRI). Methods After image-quality screening, sMRI slices were processed using Canny edge detection, brain-region cropping, 224 × 224 resizing, and augmentation. Images were organized into sex-based four-class, age-based four-class, and combined age-and-sex eight-class datasets, separating child, young, juvenile, adult, male, and female groups. A Batch-Normalized Grid-Optimized CNN (BN-GO-CNN) was developed to learn structural representations directly from preprocessed sMRI, with grid search used to select key CNN hyperparameters. The model was compared with VGG16, DenseNet201, MobileNetV2, and EfficientNet-B0 using identical image partitions. Results BN-GO-CNN achieved validation accuracies of 67.0 %, 64.0 %, and 60.5 % for sex-based, age-based, and combined age-and-sex classification, respectively. These outcomes remained above chance but showed limited class separability. Conclusions The modest performance suggests that label-related sMRI differences are subtle, supporting this framework as a preliminary test of CNN-assisted sMRI classification for future research use rather than a clinically reliable ASD diagnostic system.

title: Pulmonary CT classification based on CNN and Grad-CAM explainability using VGG16 and MobileNetV2.
abstract: Objectives This study compared the classification performance of VGG16 and MobileNetV2 models for normal-versus-lung-cancer-positive pulmonary CT image classification, with Grad-CAM used for post-hoc visual explainability. Methods A hospital-provided dataset of 550 non-contrast thoracic CT images, comprising 240 normal and 310 lung cancer-positive images, was divided into training, validation and test subsets using a patient-grouped stratified 50/10/40 split. Images were acquired at 120 kV with a 512 × 512 matrix using a NeuViz 128 CT scanner. Both models used the same preprocessing, training-only augmentation and evaluation protocol. The VGG16 model used stacked convolutional blocks, whereas MobileNetV2 used inverted residual bottlenecks with global average pooling, dropout and a sigmoid classification layer. Performance was assessed using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1-score, balanced accuracy, ROC-AUC, MCC and Cohen's kappa, while Grad-CAM examined decision-relevant regions. Results On the 220-image independent test set, VGG16 achieved 0.9636 accuracy, 0.9677 sensitivity, 0.9583 specificity and 0.9569 ROC-AUC. MobileNetV2 achieved 0.9909 accuracy, 0.9919 sensitivity, 0.9896 specificity and 0.9858 ROC-AUC, with fewer false-positive and false-negative predictions. Conclusions MobileNetV2 achieved stronger held-out test performance than VGG16 under identical experimental conditions. Larger multi-centre patient-level validation remains necessary before clinical deployment in CT screening workflows.

title: Clinical integration of artificial intelligence for diagnosis, risk prediction and management of rare cardiovascular diseases.
abstract: RCDs comprise a diverse group of inherited and acquired disorders characterized by low prevalence, substantial genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity, delayed diagnosis, and limited evidence-based therapeutic options. These challenges contribute to poor clinical outcomes, including progressive heart failure, malignant arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death. This review summarizes recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) for the diagnosis and management of RCDs. AI technologies, including machine learning, deep learning, and multimodal data integration, enable comprehensive analysis of electrocardiography, echocardiography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, computed tomography, genomic and multi-omics data, biomarkers, wearable devices, and electronic health records. These approaches improve early disease detection, phenotypic classification, risk stratification, prognostic prediction and personalized treatment planning. Current evidence suggests that AI significantly enhances diagnostic accuracy, prognostic assessment, and individualized clinical decision-making in patients with RCDs. Future clinical implementation requires standardized multicenter datasets, prospective validation, transparent and explainable algorithms, robust regulatory and ethical frameworks, and seamless integration into healthcare systems. Continued interdisciplinary collaboration will accelerate AI-driven precision cardiovascular medicine and improve outcomes for patients with rare cardiovascular diseases.

These challenges contribute to poor clinical outcomes, including progressive heart failure, malignant arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death. This review summarizes recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) for the diagnosis and management of RCDs. AI technologies, including machine learning, deep learning, and multimodal data integration, enable comprehensive analysis of electrocardiography, echocardiography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, computed tomography, genomic and multi-omics data, biomarkers, wearable devices, and electronic health records. These approaches improve early disease detection, phenotypic classification, risk stratification, prognostic prediction and personalized treatment planning. Current evidence suggests that AI significantly enhances diagnostic accuracy, prognostic assessment, and individualized clinical decision-making in patients with RCDs. Future clinical implementation requires standardized multicenter datasets, prospective validation, transparent and explainable algorithms, robust regulatory and ethical frameworks, and seamless integration into healthcare systems. Continued interdisciplinary collaboration will accelerate AI-driven precision cardiovascular medicine and improve outcomes for patients with rare cardiovascular diseases.

title: Pediatric prolactinoma-associated pituitary apoplexy presenting with acute visual loss: a case report, literature review, and management strategy.
abstract: Objectives Hemorrhagic pituitary apoplexy (PA) in children is exceedingly rare, with approximately 32 cases reported since 1980. Current guidelines recommend cabergoline as first-line therapy; however, acute complete visual loss mandates emergency surgical decompression. No guideline defines the optimal extent of resection, despite gross total resection carrying a 48-54 % risk of panhypopituitarism. Case presentation An 11-year-old prepubertal girl presented with a 2-day history of complete right-eye visual loss. Serum prolactin was 987 μg/L, and MRI demonstrated a hemorrhagic sellar-suprasellar mass compressing the optic chiasm. Emergency endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery was performed with an intentionally limited strategy - hematoma evacuation, optic decompression, and partial debulking - deliberately avoiding aggressive capsular dissection. Histopathology confirmed prolactinoma. Vision was fully restored immediately after extubation, with near-complete visual field recovery on postoperative day 5 (VFI 98 %). Adrenocortical function was preserved. Central hypothyroidism developed, and levothyroxine was initiated. Cabergoline (0.25 mg/week) was started on postoperative day 5, achieving a 93.7 % prolactin reduction by day 20 (987 → 61.9 μg/L). Conclusions In pediatric prolactinoma-associated PA requiring emergency surgery, a decompression-first strategy prioritizing visual rescue and tissue diagnosis over gross total resection may reduce the risk of panhypopituitarism, with residual tumor subsequently managed with cabergoline. The rapid biochemical response documented here supports this approach, though multicenter prospective evaluation is required.

An 11-year-old prepubertal girl presented with a 2-day history of complete right-eye visual loss. title: Lung ultrasound B-lines and serum KL-6 in the management of connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease.
abstract: Interstitial lung disease (ILD) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with connective tissue diseases (CTDs). Early diagnosis, appropriate intervention, and close monitoring are critical to mitigate the progression of CTD-ILD. Lung ultrasound (LUS) B-lines and serum Krebs von den Lungen-6 (KL-6) have emerged as promising, non-invasive, and radiation-free biomarkers for ILD. This single-center retrospective study aimed to evaluate the combined diagnostic and assessment value of B-lines and KL-6 in patients with CTD-ILD. A total of 226 consecutive patients with CTD who underwent high resolution computed tomography (HRCT), LUS and serum KL-6 testing within a one-month interval were retrospectively enrolled. Based on HRCT findings, patients were classified into ILD and non-ILD groups. Those with ILD were further subdivided into fibrotic ILD (F-ILD) and non-fibrotic ILD (NF-ILD) according to radiographic patterns. LUS was performed across 50 scanning sites, and the total number of B-lines was calculated as a B-lines number. Correlations between B-lines number, KL-6 level, and HRCT Warrick score were analyzed. The diagnostic accuracy of LUS B-lines and KL-6, individually and in combination, for detecting ILD and F-ILD was determined using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. The ability of B-lines and KL-6 to discriminate ILD severity based on the HRCT Warrick score was assessed. The ILD group demonstrated significantly higher B-lines number and serum KL-6 levels compared to the non-ILD group (P < 0.001). ROC analysis showed good diagnostic performance for both B-lines (AUC = 0.85 [95% CI: 0.80-0.90]; sensitivity = 77.6%; specificity = 77.0%) and KL-6 (AUC = 0.79 [95% CI: 0.73-0.85]; sensitivity = 58.6%; specificity = 91.9%). The combination of both markers further improved diagnostic accuracy (AUC = 0.87 [95% CI: 0.82-0.91]; sensitivity = 74.3%; specificity = 86.5%). Both B-lines number and KL-6 level showed significant positive correlations with the HRCT Warrick score. Notably, B-lines number and serum KL-6 were able to distinguish between F-ILD and NF-ILD subtypes (both P < 0.001) and were associated with disease severity (P < 0.001 for B-lines; P = 0.016 for KL-6). Both LUS B-lines and serum KL-6 are valuable biomarkers for diagnosing and assessing CTD-ILD, and their combination enhances diagnostic accuracy.

title: Regional Brain Structural Changes During the Transition from Acute to Chronic Neuropathic Pain: A Longitudinal Study in a Rat Model of Orofacial Pain.
abstract: Brain imaging studies have identified structural alterations in individuals with chronic neuropathic pain, particularly in regions involved in sensory, emotional, and cognitive processing. However, most studies remain cross-sectional, leaving the temporal progression of these changes during pain chronification unclear. This gap is critical, as both neural and non-neural cells undergo dynamic changes during pain chronification. The primary aim of this study was to track longitudinally regional brain volume and density changes before and after induction of orofacial neuropathic pain in male rats, using a chronic constriction injury of the infraorbital nerve (ION-CCI). This model enables assessment of changes in the spinal trigeminal nucleus (SpVn). T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging scans were acquired 7 d prior to injury and then at +2, +7, +14, and +28 d, in ION-CCI ( n = 11), sham-injured ( n = 6), and naive ( n = 8) groups. Voxel-based and deformation-based morphometry were used to identify early- and late-onset density and volumetric changes, respectively. Early after injury, transient, bidirectional volume and/or density changes in the ipsilateral primary somatosensory cortex (S1), contralateral SpVn, and bilateral dorsomedial periaqueductal gray, ipsilateral retrosplenial and contralateral prelimbic cortices, were observed. In contrast, late-onset changes were more widespread, with volume increases observed bilaterally in the SpVn pars interpolaris (SpVo), in the ipsilateral dorsomedial SpVn (SpVdm), bilateral lateral hypothalamus, and contralateral amygdalo-hippocampal complex, and volume decreases in contralateral retrosplenial, prelimbic, and bilateral S1 cortices. These findings reveal early dynamic reorganization of sensory and sensory-modulatory brain regions, followed by sustained structural alterations across trigeminal brainstem nuclei, limbic-hypothalamic systems, and higher-order cortical networks.

title: Intracranial germ cell tumours presenting with AVP deficiency and evolving panhypopituitarism: diagnostic pitfalls in early imaging and biopsy.
abstract: We report three Chinese children with central nervous system germ cell tumours (CNS GCTs) presenting as arginine vasopressin (AVP) deficiency with or without pituitary stalk thickening, initially diagnosed as lymphocytic hypophysitis (LyH) and idiopathic AVP deficiency. Case 1 showed conflicting biopsy results, suggesting hypophysitis and then germinoma. Case 2 had one negative transsphenoidal biopsy and later one biopsy finding LyH before suprasellar mass diagnosis. Case 3 had a normal initial MRI brain and was followed up as idiopathic AVP deficiency but found to have extensive tumour the next year. All patients achieved remission with chemotherapy and radiotherapy but sustained lifelong panhypopituitarism. Asia has a higher prevalence of CNS GCTs in children. Pituitary stalk thickening with risk factors including pituitary stalk thickness ≥6.5 mm, AVP deficiency, two or more pituitary hormone deficiencies at presentation, and evolving hypopituitarism mandates a high level of malignant suspicion even if prior histopathology is negative. In ethnic groups where the prevalence of CNS GCT is higher, biopsy should be offered when presented with risk factors. These cases highlight pitfalls of false-negative MRI and biopsy, emphasising epidemiology-informed diagnostic algorithms to prevent diagnostic delays.

title: A review of digital orthopedic techniques in pre- and intra-operative management of scaphoid fracture.
abstract: Digital orthopedics integrates artificial intelligence, finite element analysis, virtual surgical planning, intraoperative navigation, robotics, and three-dimensional printing into a precise, individualized workflow for scaphoid fracture management. Artificial intelligence-based algorithms achieve high diagnostic accuracy for scaphoid fractures on plain radiographs, aid in detecting occult fractures, and support treatment decisions. Three-dimensional fracture mapping and finite element analysis enable quantitative assessment of fracture morphology and biomechanical stability, supporting individualized preoperative planning. Computer-assisted navigation reduces radiation exposure and guidewire attempts compared with conventional fluoroscopy but remains limited by registration inaccuracy and dependence on manual execution. Robot-assisted surgery improves procedural consistency and screw accuracy, with a learning curve of approximately 10-20 cases; however, it is constrained by longer setup times, high costs, and predominantly level IV evidence. Virtual surgical planning combined with three-dimensional printing provides patient-specific percutaneous guides, reduction templates, anatomical models, and custom prostheses, improving accuracy, reducing radiation exposure, and enabling motion-preserving salvage for scaphoid nonunions and scaphoid nonunion advanced collapse. Current evidence is largely based on small case series and cadaveric studies, highlighting the need for standardized protocols and high-quality comparative trials to support widespread adoption.

title: Management of Nondiagnostic Thyroid Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology Nodules Based on TI-RADS Risk Assessment.
abstract: Objective The high prevalence of thyroid nodules and the frequent occurrence of nondiagnostic (ND) results on fine-needle aspiration (FNA) necessitates malignancy risk stratification to balance cancer detection while avoiding unnecessary repeat biopsies. This study evaluated malignancy rates and management strategies for nodules with ND cytology, stratified by the American College of Radiology Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (TI-RADS) score. Methods This retrospective study analyzed 342 consecutive patients with initial ND ultrasound-guided (USG) thyroid FNA from a high volume, two-practitioner clinic between January 2019 and June 2024. Data collected from chart review included Bethesda cytopathology classifications, management approaches, and final histopathological diagnosis when available. Results Among 3717 thyroid FNAs performed during the study period, 342 (9.2%) were ND on initial sampling. TI-RADS (TR) distribution for ND nodules was: TR1 9.6%, TR2 9.9%, TR3 28.1%, TR4 45.3%, TR5 7.0%. Initial management comprised repeat FNA in 170 (49.7%) patients, ultrasound (US) surveillance in 101 (29.5%), surgery in 17 (5.0%); 54 (15.8%) patients were lost to follow-up. Of repeat FNAs, 47 (27.6%) remained ND. Among 33 surgical cases, malignancy was identified in 6 (1.8%) index nodules with initial ND cytology. Five malignancies occurred in TR4 nodules and one in a TR5 nodule. Importantly, there were no malignancies among 17 resected TR1-3 nodules. Conclusion For experienced practitioners in a high-volume clinic, ND thyroid FNA cytology carries a low overall observed risk of malignancy (1.8%). TI-RADS scores should be taken into consideration to guide management decisions for ND cytology nodules between repeat FNA, US surveillance, or surgery.

title: [Breast implant-associated squamous cell carcinoma].
abstract: Numerous clinical studies and experimental findings have confirmed that breast implants with different textures and fillings can promote structural changes in cells and tissues within the implant capsule, which may induce tumorigenesis in the long term. Breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL) and squamous cell carcinoma (BIA-SCC) are two distinct malignant conditions that develop within the implant capsule and are clearly distinct from breast cancer; their estimated incidence and prevalence are low. Recognized by the WHO since 2023, BIA-SCC is an immunological inflammatory process associated with chronic antigen stimulation, where the actual risk of tumor development and its triggering factors remain unclear, but the investigation of tumor-associated genetic mutations and environmental influences remains at the center of scientific interest. Systemic symptoms of immunodeficiency (fever, chronic fatigue, weakness) are less prominent in the presence of CK5/6 and p40/p63 positivity. Local symptoms (late seroma, painful breast swelling, asymmetry, capsule thickening, skin symptoms) dominate and typically appear 15-20 years after implantation. Positive cytology and immunohistochemistry results following imaging studies (ultrasound, MRI, fine-needle aspiration biopsy, CT, PET/CT) indicate a good prognosis in localized cases. In 80% of patients diagnosed with BIA-SCC, extracapsular tumor invasion is already evident at the time of diagnosis. The aggressiveness of BIA-SCC is demonstrated by the fact that the 6-month mortality rate in registered cases was very high, at 43.8%. Care must be provided with mandatory multidisciplinary professional involvement, and data recording is mandatory in every country; in Hungary, there is a reporting obligation to the Implant Registry of the National Health Insurance Fund Administration. Beyond plastic surgery and oncology research, all physicians must be aware of the importance of monitoring the signs and symptoms of patients with breast implants and, in cases of clinical suspicion, referring patients for appropriate diagnostic testing. This study summarizes our current knowledge regarding the epidemiological factors of BIA-SCC, its pathogenesis, genetic and clinical aspects, treatment, and prognosis. Orv Hetil. 2026; 167(40): 1585-1592.

title: Umbilical cord blood miR-125b-5p: a diagnostic and prognostic biomarker for neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.
abstract: Objective Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS) is a common respiratory disease. This study aimed to detect the expression of miR-125b-5p in the umbilical cord blood of NRDS patients and to evaluate its diagnostic and prognostic value. Methods Fluorescence-based real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction was used to detect miR-125b-5p expression in the umbilical cord blood of NRDS patients and controls. The correlation between miR-125b-5p expression and NRDS clinical data was analyzed. Survival was analyzed using the Kaplan-Meier method. Cox regression identified risk factors for adverse outcomes, and the ROC curve evaluated diagnostic and prognostic accuracy. Results The level of miR-125b-5p in NRDS patients was higher than that in controls. High miR-125b-5p expression was correlated with C-reactive protein levels, umbilical artery blood gas parameters, and the lung ultrasound score. Patients with high miR-125b-5p expression had significantly shorter event-free survival (HR 2.358, 95%CI 1.345-4.133, p<0.05) and long-term survival (HR 2.489, 95%CI 1.201-5.161, p<0.05). Cox regression identified high miR-125b-5p expression, high lung ultrasound score, high PaCO₂, and high PaO₂ as prognostic factors. Conclusions Umbilical cord blood miR-125b-5p is highly expressed in NRDS. It may serve as a biomarker for the diagnosis and prognosis of NRDS.

title: A multidisciplinary diagnostic approach to thoracic endometriosis syndrome: Insights from CT imaging, surgery, and pathology.
abstract: Background Thoracic endometriosis syndrome (TES) is the most common extrapelvic manifestation of endometriosis, yet its classification, diagnosis, and treatment remain debated. Thoracic endometriosis syndrome has recently been proposed to be categorized into 3 types: pleural, bronchopulmonary, and diaphragmatic. Objectives Our study aims to propose a 3-step approach - computed tomography (CT) imaging, careful intraoperative assessment, and targeted pathology - to enhance the diagnostic process and optimize the management of TES-related pneumothorax. Material and methods We retrospectively analyzed 3 cases of recurrent right-sided catamenial pneumothorax in female patients with a history of pelvic endometriosis, managed surgically at the Department of Thoracic Surgery, Medical University of Gdansk, between 2021 and 2024. All included patients underwent video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS), with comprehensive preoperative CT imaging, intraoperative lesion mapping, and postoperative histopathological examination, improving diagnostic accuracy in TES, with a possible impact on therapeutic results. Results Chest CT is essential for detecting bullous lesions, aiding in intraoperative identification and surgical treatment. Immunohistochemistry (IHC), assessing estrogen receptor (ER) and CD10 for stromal identification, improves pathological accuracy. Conclusions This study underlines the diagnostic value of integrating imaging, intraoperative assessment, and targeted histopathology, as well as clear communication between surgeons, radiologists, and pathologists to ensure accurate diagnosis and an improved therapeutic process for patients in clinical practice.

title: Ischemic colitis associated with oral semaglutide with recurrence upon rechallenge.
abstract: Ischemic colitis associated with glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists is an exceptionally rare condition, with only a few cases reported in the literature. We present the case of a 46-year-old woman treated with oral semaglutide (Rybelsus®) for weight loss who experienced three episodes of abdominal pain and hematochezia temporally associated with drug exposure. The third episode, which occurred after semaglutide was reintroduced, led to a confirmed diagnosis based on computed tomography, rectosigmoidoscopy, and histopathological findings consistent with ischemic colitis. Permanent discontinuation of semaglutide was followed by complete clinical resolution without further recurrence. The temporal relationship, improvement after drug withdrawal, and recurrence upon rechallenge support a probable causal association. This case highlights the need to consider ischemic colitis as a potential rare adverse effect of semaglutide.

title: Jejunal Dieulafoy's lesion: challenging diagnosis and treatment, and an even greater challenge for clinical pathways.
abstract: Regarding the article by João Carlos Gonçalves et al. on a rare case of Dieulafoy's lesion in an atypical jejunal location, we would like to highlight the potential of real-time capsule viewing, integrated into a dedicated clinical pathway allowing early device-assisted enteroscopy. The identification of an active bleeding during within the first hour after pyloric passage of emergency real-time capsule may help select the most appropriate approach for emergency enteroscopy, usually the oral route in this setting, and may increase the diagnostic yield and endoscopic therapy. Once the patient has been hemodynamically stabilized, such a strategy requires a dedicated and streamlined clinical pathway for emergency DAE, including prompt access to a specialized endoscopy unit, appropriately trained staff, and the resources required for deep sedation or general anesthesia. The same pathway should also anticipate early rebleeding after endoscopic therapy. In our experience, rebleeding may occur in up to 25% of cases, most frequently within the first 48 hours.

title: Giant hepatic angiomylipoma presenting with painful hepatomegaly.
abstract: Hepatic angiomyolipoma (HAML) is a rare mesenchymal neoplasm belonging to the perivascular epithelioid cell tumor (PEComa) family. Although usually asymptomatic and incidentally detected, large lesions may cause symptoms and pose diagnostic challenges. We report the case of a 69-year-old man presenting with painful hepatomegaly. Computed tomography revealed a 12-cm, predominantly fat-containing hepatic mass. Percutaneous biopsy demonstrated characteristic morphological features and an immunohistochemical profile showing HMB-45 and Melan-A positivity, with negative S100 and smooth muscle actin staining in the epithelioid tumor cells. Surgical resection was performed, with a favorable postoperative course. This case highlights the importance of integrating radiological and histopathological findings for accurate diagnosis and individualized management of giant hepatic angiomyolipoma.

title: [Constrictive pericarditis is a rare disease and often idiopathic].
abstract: Case A 46-year-old female presented to her general practitioner with abdominal pain, lethargy, dyspnea and pedal edema. Computed tomography (CT) revealed features of heart and liver failure with pleural fluid and ascites and the liver having a cirrhotic appearance. A gastroenterologist confirmed the diagnosis of cirrhosis, but the etiology was unknown. Pericardial calcifications and elevated jugular venous pressure on examination gave rise to a suspicion of constrictive pericarditis as the cause of the liver cirrhosis. Cardiac catheterization confirmed pericardial constriction, and the patient underwent a total pericardiectomy. Discussion It is easy to miss a diagnosis of constrictive pericarditis because it must be specifically sought after in the echocardiogram, and pericardial calcifications are only present in a minority of cases.

title: A white-light endoscopy-based mixed-effects nomogram for predicting small colorectal polyp neoplasia in resource-limited settings.
abstract: Introduction Accurate optical characterization of small colorectal polyps relies on narrow-band imaging (NBI) or artificial intelligence, both of which are unavailable in resource-limited settings. Objectives We aimed to develop and validate a web-based nomogram using white-light endoscopy (WLE) and routine clinical variables to predict neoplastic polyp histology. Patients and methods This prospective single-center study (Vietnam, September 2020-April 2021) included 301 patients with 451 small colorectal polyps (≤10 mm). Polyps were assessed in real time using WLE and NBI before histological confirmation. Data were split at the patient level into training (254 patients, 383 polyps) and validation (47 patients, 68 polyps) cohorts. L1-penalized generalized linear mixed-effects models were used for feature selection and model development. Results Neoplastic histology was present in 55.9% of polyps. Four predictors were identified: sessile/pedunculated morphology (0-Is/0-Ip), age ≥50 years, polyp size >5 mm, and neoplastic WLE diagnosis. In internal validation, the WLE+3F model achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.849, outperforming WLE alone (AUC, 0.760; P = 0.009) and comparable with NBI (AUC, 0.858; P = 0.86), with sensitivity of 65.8%, specificity of 90.0%, and good calibration (Brier score, 0.160). Decision curve analysis showed clinical net benefit. Conclusions A WLE-based nomogram combined with 3 clinical factors achieved performance comparable with NBI, offering an accessible tool for real-time risk stratification in resource-limited settings; external validation is warranted.

title: Hierarchical Reasoning Gates for Multimodal Large Language Models in Dental Image Interpretation: A Prompt-Level Protocol for Improving Accuracy
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have been used to support dental image interpretation, but performance may depend on prompt structure. We proposed Hierarchical Reasoning Gates (HRG), a prompt-level protocol organizing image interpretation into sequential stages with validation before progression. Forty anonymized panoramic radiographs of impacted mandibular molars were analyzed using three prompt architectures: P1, zero-shot natural language; P2, a five-step structured workflow followed by a final internal-validation checkpoint; and P3, HRG with 10 macro-stages and 35 procedural control blocks. Outputs were compared with expert radiology reference reports using five predefined variables. Mean Total Score was 3.52 ± 0.85, 3.58 ± 0.71, and 4.35 ± 0.74 for P1, P2, and P3, respectively; Full Accuracy was 10.0%, 5.0%, and 50.0%. Reports with errors in three or more variables occurred in 12.5%, 7.5%, and 0%, respectively. Only Apparent Anatomical Relationship differed significantly across prompts after Holm adjustment. Test–retest repeatability was high for several variables but lower for Apparent Anatomical Relationship in P3. HRG was associated with higher image-interpretation performance and fewer complex error patterns, although higher performance did not uniformly translate into greater repeatability. These findings support gated prompt design for controlling dependent steps in MLLM-based image analysis, while clinical use still requires expert supervision.

title: Seven Novel Sonographic Signs
abstract: Ultrasound is a widely used imaging modality in clinical practice, and sonographic signs serve as valuable teaching tools that aid in pattern recognition and diagnosis. This review consolidates five novel sonographic signs previously proposed by the author, including the Cracked Earth Sign for subcutaneous edema, the Mushroom Cap Sign for localized gallbladder adenomyomatosis, the LTS Sign for dilated cardiomyopathy, the LTI Sign for endocardial fibroelastosis, and the Three Pipes Sign for the suprasternal long-axis view of the aortic arch. The SFH Sign for advanced cervical insufficiency and the Gentle Wave Sign for the tardus-parvus waveform are proposed for the first time in this paper. Collectively, these seven signs span the fields of superficial ultrasound, abdominal ultrasound, echocardiography, and obstetric ultrasound. For each sign, its naming logic, definition, clinical implications, and teaching value are described. This review aims to facilitate a better understanding of these signs and to promote their use as teaching aids in ultrasound education.

title: Deep Survival Analysis: A Comprehensive Review of Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges in Biomedicine
abstract: Survival analysis is fundamental to biomedical research and clinical decision-making, where outcomes such as mortality, disease progression, relapse, and time-to-discharge are frequently observed under censoring and competing risks. Recent advances in deep learning have expanded the capabilities of survival modeling by enabling flexible nonlinear representations of heterogeneous biomedical data, including electronic health records, medical imaging, and multi-omics profiles. This structured narrative review synthesizes studies published between 2018 and 2026, examining major deep survival model families, including neural extensions of the Cox proportional hazards model, discrete-time and distribution-based approaches, multimodal architectures, transformers, and emerging foundation-model paradigms. We critically compare deep learning approaches with classical and machine learning survival methods, highlighting the conditions under which increased model complexity provides meaningful advantages. We further examine representative biomedical applications, datasets, evaluation and benchmarking practices, with particular emphasis on calibration, competing risks, external validation, and model selection. The review identifies persistent challenges in generalization, sample size and event scarcity, censoring mechanisms, interpretability, fairness, reproducibility, and clinical translation, while outlining emerging directions toward robust, trustworthy, and clinically actionable survival modeling systems.

title: Vascular and Circulating Blood Exposure to Proton or Photon Irradiation: Differentials in Lymphocyte Subsets Metrics in Cancer Patients
abstract: Background: /Objectives: Radiation-induced lymphopenia is consistently associated with adverse outcomes across solid tumours, yet the vascular compartment that carries the irradiated lym-phocyte pool is not common delineated during treatment planning. The VASA project makes blood vessels an explicit, measurable structure in that process. We report Phase II, relating dose–volume metrics computed on MRI-segmented vessels to serial immunophenotyping in patients treated with protons or photons. Methods: Forty-three patients treated between March 2021, and May 2022 were studied prospectively (35 proton, 8 photon). Flow-contrast three-dimensional MRI with three velocity-encoding directions was added to simulation; the sum-of-magnitude recon-struction was used for semi-automated vessel segmentation, and vessel masks were imported into the treatment planning system to generate dose–volume histograms. The effective dose to circu-lating immune cells (EDIC), the integral dose to vessels (IDVe) and the integral dose to target were computed. Blood was sampled at the start, middle and end of irradiation for lymphocyte counts and B, T and NK immunophenotyping. Results: EDIC and IDVe were higher with photons than protons (6.10 vs. 1.22 Gy; 3.6 vs. 0.5 Gy·L) and higher in patients who became lymphopenic than in those who did not (4.2 vs. 1.1 Gy; 2.7 vs. 0.37 Gy·L). Within the proton cohort, EDIC and IDVe increased from brain to head-and-neck to thorax–abdomen targets (0.80, 1.11 and 1.89 Gy; 0.15, 0.26 and 1.31 Gy·L; p < 0.05). Lymphocyte counts fell from 1.81 to 1.42 × 10³/µL overall (p < 0.05), with the lowest nadir in thorax–abdomen targets (0.90 × 10³/µL). B, T and NK subpopula-tions all declined; T and NK losses were greatest in head-and-neck targets. Conclusions: Vascular dose can be measured patient by patient and tracks both irradiation modality and the magnitude of lymphocyte depletion. Treating vessels and circulating blood as an organ at risk is feasible and offers a route to immune-sparing radiotherapy plan optimisation.

title: Qualitative Dynamic Contrast-Enhanced MRI Time–Intensity Curve Analysis for Differentiating Non-Progressive Treatment-Related Changes from Tumor Progression After Stereotactic Radiotherapy for Brain Metastases
abstract: Background: This exploratory study assessed whether qualitative dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI (DCE-MRI) time–intensity curves (TICs) differentiate non-progressive treatment-related changes (NPTRC) from tumor recurrence after stereotactic radiotherapy for brain metastases. Methods: Thirty-two patients with 51 treated lesions underwent DCE-MRI. Five neuroradiologists inde-pendently delineated a volume of interest and classified the resulting TIC as Type A–D. Longitudinal clinical and MRI follow-up provided the reference outcome, which was recorded before the TIC framework was finalized. An A/B versus C/D grouping was evaluated as a secondary exploratory analysis. Results: Thirty-five lesions were classified as NPTRC and 16 as tumor recurrence. All 17 Type A lesions were NPTRC, and all 13 Type C/D lesions showed recurrence. Type B occurred in both groups (18 NPTRC; 3 recurrences). The A/B versus C/D grouping yielded 81.3% sensitivity and 100% specificity. The ordinal TIC analysis yielded an area under the curve of 0.952. Interobserver agree-ment was high for the four TIC categories (Fleiss’ κ = 0.889). Conclusions: Type A was associated with NPTRC, Types C/D with recurrence, and Type B represented an indeterminate pattern. These descriptive findings require independent validation before clinical use.

title: Binding Text to Pixels: A Narrative Review of Supervision Granularity in Language-Guided Chest Radiograph Segmentation and Grounding
abstract: Chest radiography is the most common diagnostic X-ray examination, and paired images and reports are abundant in routine care, yet lesion-level spatial annotation remains scarce. This structured narrative review examines how radiology text has been used to supervise localization in chest radiographs: phrase grounding, weakly supervised abnormality localization, language-guided segmentation, grounded report generation, and multimodal large language models with spatial reasoning. Literature was drawn from a Web of Science seed search, citation chaining, and targeted searches through September 2026, and is organized along one axis, the granularity at which text binds to pixels, in five levels from study-level alignment to promptable or generative grounding. We show the axis is better read as two: train-time binding and inference-time spatial output come apart, and the systems that decouple them are the informative ones. Benchmarks such as MS-CXR and PadChest-GR made local evaluation realistic, and anatomy-aware resources such as PAXRay indicate that structural supervision improves grounding. Lesion masks now exist for the largest report corpus but are derived from those same reports, so model and reference share failure modes. We argue that anatomy-referenced evaluation, computable today, is the most tractable near-term correction, and that cross-study score comparison remains unsafe.

title: Exploring the Association Between Breast Cancer Perception and Health-Promoting Lifestyle Behaviours Among Women: A Cross-Sectional Study in Saudi Arabia
abstract: Aim: To examine breast cancer perception, health-promoting lifestyle behaviours, and screening practices, and their sociodemographic and psychosocial correlates, among women in Abha, Saudi Arabia. Methods: A cross-sectional survey of 1,002 women aged ≥18 years in Abha (May–December 2025), recruited online through social media and instant messaging. Validated Arabic versions of the Breast Cancer Perception Scale (BCPS) and HPLP-II were self-administered online, with self-reported breast self-examination (BSE), clinical breast examination (CBE), and mammography history. Multiple linear regression identified predictors of HPLP-II and BCPS scores. Results: Perceived knowledge (3.64 ± 1.05), treatment belief (3.43 ± 0.77), fear (3.25 ± 1.30), and perceived risk (3.40 ± 0.89) were moderately high; perceived need for health checks (2.78 ± 1.23) and stigma (2.89 ± 1.14) were lower. HPLP-II mean was 2.63 ± 0.46 (spiritual growth highest 2.96 ± 0.50; physical ac-tivity lowest 2.23 ± 0.60). Ever-screening: BSE 61.1% (95% CI 58.1–64.1), CBE 22.5% (95% CI 20.0–25.1), mammography 12.8% (95% CI 10.8–14.8). Perceived knowledge (β = 0.059), treatment belief (β = 0.120), and stigma (β = 0.058) were positively, and perceived need for health checks (β = −0.259), perceived risk (β = −0.130), and fear (β = −0.028) negatively, associated with HPLP-II. Married women had higher lifestyle and perception scores; more educated and publicly employed women had higher perception scores. Conclusion: Despite moderately high perceived knowledge, clinical screening particularly mammography remains very low, and physical activity, a modifiable breast cancer risk factor, is the weakest lifestyle do-main. Awareness alone does not translate into screening; interventions should address fear and symptom-contingent care-seeking, embed screening referral in primary care, involve families, and promote culturally appropriate physical activity.

title: A Controlled Benchmark of Deep Segmentation Architectures for Mammographic Microcalcification Segmentation on CBIS-DDSM: Evidence Consistent with an Annotation-Related Performance Limit
abstract: Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer in women worldwide, and clustered microcalcifications on mammography are among its earliest indicators. Automated segmentation of microcalcifications is challenging because the calcifications are small, sparse, and often embedded in dense fibroglandular tissue. In addition, publicly available datasets such as CBIS-DDSM provide annotations at the calcification-cluster level rather than for individual calcification particles. Although numerous deep-learning architectures have been proposed for this task, their relative performance under a common experimental framework remains unclear. This study presents a rigorous, leakage-controlled benchmark of ten segmentation architectures, including convolutional models (U-Net, nnU-Net, BreastNet, ConvNeXt-UNet), an attention-gated model (Attention U-Net), convolution-transformer hybrids (TransUNet, Swin-UNet, MedFormer, UNETR), and MAFT-Net, a multi-scale attention network incorporating dilated convolutions, squeeze-and-excitation gating, self-attention, and gated feature fusion. All models were trained from scratch using identical preprocessing, augmentation, optimisation, and patient-disjoint train/test partitions on the CBIS-DDSM calcification subset. Performance was evaluated using Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), Intersection-over-Union (IoU), 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95), sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and classification AUC. Across all architectures, Dice scores were confined to a narrow range (0.076-0.114), with most pairwise differences failing to reach statistical significance. Increasing architectural complexity, including transformer-based models containing up to 89 million parameters, did not produce consistent performance gains. ROI occupancy analysis showed a strong positive association between Dice and annotation size, with mean Dice increasing from 0.023 to 0.255 across occupancy quartiles. These findings suggest that segmentation performance on CBIS-DDSM is influenced more by the region-level annotation format than by architectural innovation, highlighting an important limitation when interpreting reported overlap metrics.

title: Case Series Analysis of Five Rare Cases of Hyperprolactinemia in Diabetes Mellitus: Clinical Characteristics, Molecular Pathways, and Implications for Targeted Management
abstract: Background: Hyperprolactinemia, characterized by serum prolactin levels >20 ng/mL, is a rare comorbidity in diabetes mellitus, potentially exacerbating insulin resistance and glycemic dysregulation via JAK/STAT signaling. This case series analysis examines five rare cases to elucidate clinical patterns, molecular mechanisms, and therapeutic outcomes, aiming to inform precision endocrine management. Methods: Five cases were curated from PubMed and Scopus (1999–2025), focusing on hyperprolactinemia in diabetes (type 1, type 2, or insipidus). Data on demographics, symptoms, laboratory findings (prolactin, insulin, C-peptide), imaging (MRI), and treatment outcomes were extracted. Results: The cohort included 3 females and 2 males (mean age: 26.2 years, range: 7–33). Prolactin levels ranged from 145–3,177 ng/mL, with 2/5 cases (40%) having type 1 diabetes, 1/5 (20%) type 2, 1/5 (20%) diabetes insipidus, and 1/5 (20%) factitious hypoglycemia. Presentations included hypogonadism (3/5, 60%), galactorrhea (2/5, 40%), and hypoglycemia (2/5, 40%). MRI revealed microadenomas (2/5, 40%), a macroadenoma (1/5, 20%), or normal pituitary (2/5, 40%). Cabergoline or medication withdrawal normalized prolactin in 4/5 (80%), reducing levels (e.g., 3,177 to 321 ng/mL in one case) and improving glycemic control (fewer hypoglycemic episodes) in 3/5 (60%). Prolactin activates JAK2/STAT5, inducing SOCS3 to inhibit IRS-1/PI3K/Akt, impairing glucose uptake. Conclusion: Hyperprolactinemia, whether tumoral or non-tumoral, disrupts metabolic homeostasis in diabetes. Routine prolactin screening is recommended for patients with reproductive or glycemic anomalies, emphasizing targeted therapies like dopamine agonists to optimize outcomes.

Results:

The cohort included 3 females and 2 males (mean age: 26.2 years, range: 7–33). Prolactin levels ranged from 145–3,177 ng/mL, with 2/5 cases (40%) having type 1 diabetes, 1/5 (20%) type 2, 1/5 (20%) diabetes insipidus, and 1/5 (20%) factitious hypoglycemia. Presentations included hypogonadism (3/5, 60%), galactorrhea (2/5, 40%), and hypoglycemia (2/5, 40%). MRI revealed microadenomas (2/5, 40%), a macroadenoma (1/5, 20%), or normal pituitary (2/5, 40%). Cabergoline or medication withdrawal normalized prolactin in 4/5 (80%), reducing levels (e.g., 3,177 to 321 ng/mL in one case) and improving glycemic control (fewer hypoglycemic episodes) in 3/5 (60%). Prolactin activates JAK2/STAT5, inducing SOCS3 to inhibit IRS-1/PI3K/Akt, impairing glucose uptake.

Conclusion:

Hyperprolactinemia, whether tumoral or non-tumoral, disrupts metabolic homeostasis in diabetes. Routine prolactin screening is recommended for patients with reproductive or glycemic anomalies, emphasizing targeted therapies like dopamine agonists to optimize outcomes.

title: Clinical Applications of Metabolomics in Paediatric Brain Tumours and Other Solid Tumours: A Review
abstract: There is growing interest in utilising metabolomics as a tool in childhood cancer research. We propose four main applications of metabolomics in this context; as a less invasive diagnostic technique, to identify prognostic biomarkers, to monitor disease progression or detect relapse and to identify novel therapeutic targets. MEDLINE, PubMed, EMBASE and Cochrane databases were searched. Studies evaluating metabolomics in paediatric brain and other solid tumours in the context of our four applications were included. Studies evaluating other ‘omics’ modalities, tumour types, outcomes or involving adults were excluded. 39 articles were included. Published evidence in brain tumours includes the potential for metabolomics to identify biomarkers from peripheral blood samples, possibly obviating the need for invasive biopsies. Additionally, magnetic resonance spectroscopy adds value to conventional magnetic resonance imaging for diagnosis and prognostication. Considering other solid tumours, metabolomics has been evaluated in neuroblastoma for risk stratification of disease and in osteosarcoma, retinoblastoma, Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma for identifying novel diagnostic biomarkers and improving understanding of tumour pathophysiology. Our review highlights the wide-ranging applications of metabolomics across paediatric brain and other solid tumours. There is an emerging role for metabolomics within research and clinical spheres to improve the diagnosis and management of childhood cancers.

title: OBESUS (OBESity UltraSound): A Multiorgan Bedside Ultrasound Framework for Obesity Phenotyping
abstract: Obesity is a heterogeneous chronic disease in which cardiometabolic and functional risks are influenced not only by total body fat but also by its anatomical distribution, ectopic fat accumulation, and skeletal muscle quality. Traditional anthropometric measurements, such as body mass index and waist circumference, fail to capture these biological differences. Point-of-care ultrasound provides a portable, radiation-free, repeatable, and widely available bedside tool for assessing multiple adipose and muscular compartments, yet a broadly standardized framework integrating these measurements into a multiorgan obesity phenotype remains lacking. We propose OBESUS (OBESity UltraSound), a pragmatic multiorgan point-of-care ultrasound framework for structured obesity phenotyping. To facilitate competency-based and stepwise implementation, OBESUS comprises two complementary tiers: OBESUS-Core evaluates abdominal subcutaneous adiposity, preperitoneal fat thickness, hepatic steatosis, and rectus femoris muscle quality, whereas OBESUS-Plus incorporates epicardial and perirenal adipose tissue as additional cardiorenal ectopic fat depots. Rather than generating a numerical score, the framework integrates these findings into four non-mutually exclusive ultrasound-derived phenotypes: metabolic, myosteatotic, epicardial adiposity, and perirenal adiposity. This narrative review describes the conceptual basis, standardized acquisition methodology, pragmatic reference thresholds, and potential clinical applications of OBESUS. The framework is intended to provide a foundation for prospective evaluation of its reproducibility, clinical validity, prognostic significance and potential utility for longitudinal monitoring.

title: Molecular PET Imaging Versus Conventional Imaging for Detection of Mandibular Metastases in Prostate Cancer: A Paired Retrospective Study
abstract: Purpose: Maxillofacial metastases from prostate cancer are accounts for 9–11% of metastatic jaw lesions. Optimal imaging for suspected maxillofacial metastases remains undefined. Conventional imaging often lacks sensitivity for early disease, while PET/CT may be limited due to physiologic tracer uptake in adjacent salivary glands. With increasing use of PET/CT in advanced prostate cancer, its diagnostic performance in the mandibular region requires further evaluation. Methods: We conducted a single-institution paired retrospective study using the prospectively maintained Mayo Clinic Advanced Prostate Cancer Registry. Patients with clinically confirmed mandibular metastases who underwent molecular PET/CT ([⁶⁸Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 or [¹¹C]choline) and conventional imaging (CT or MRI) within 1 month were included. All studies were blindly reviewed by a board-certified radiologist specialized in nuclear medicine. Detection rates, anatomic distribution, and quantitative imaging parameters were assessed. paired detection rates were compared using a one-sided exact McNemar test, with a two-sided exact test performed as a sensitivity analysis. Results: Eighteen patients with clinically confirmed mandibular metastases underwent 36 paired imaging evaluations (18 molecular PET/CT and 18 conventional studies). Median age was 70.5 years (IQR, 60–77), and median Gleason score was 8 (IQR, 7–9). At detection of mandibular metastasis, 56% of our cohort had hormone-sensitive and 44% had castration-resistant disease. Molecular PET/CT detected mandibular involvement in 18/18 patients (100%; 95% CI, 81–100%) versus 13/18 (72.2%; 95% CI, 47–90%) with conventional imaging. All five discordant cases were detected by molecular PET/CT but not conventional imaging, with no discordant cases favoring conventional imaging (one-sided exact McNemar p = 0.031; two-sided p = 0.063). Mandibular involvement was predominantly unilateral (94.4%), most commonly involving the body (50%), followed by the ramus (28%) and condyle (17%). Median SUVmax was 6.3 (IQR, 4.4–16.9) for PSMA PET/CT and 4.3 (IQR, 3.8–8.5) for choline PET/CT; median lesion volume was 5.0 mL (IQR, 1.1–11.3). Conclusions: Molecular PET/CT identified all clinically confirmed mandibular prostate cancer metastases in this paired cohort, including five cases not detected by conventional imaging. Despite physiologic tracer uptake in adjacent salivary structures, mandibular metastatic disease remained detectable on molecular imaging. These findings suggest that molecular PET/CT may provide complementary value when mandibular metastasis is suspected, particularly when conventional imaging is negative or equivocal.

title: Expander-Assisted Immediate Implant Placement in a Maxillary Lateral Incisor Site Combining Apical Bone Expansion, Supramaxillary Arch Buttress Stabilization, and Immediate Provisionalization: A Case Report
abstract: Background: Replacement of a maxillary lateral incisor is among the most demanding indications in implant dentistry. The site is typically narrow bucco-palatally, the buccal plate is frequently thin and largely bundle-bone dependent, and the aesthetic tolerance for ridge collapse is minimal. Immediate (Type 1) placement shortens treatment and preserves the soft-tissue architecture, but it does not prevent the remodelling of the buccal wall that follows extraction, and the osteotomy itself risks fenestration or loss of primary stability. Case presentation. A 60-year-old male smoker (about 20 cigarettes/day) with a history of stage IV periodontitis presented with an unrestorable, almost circumferential carious lesion of the maxillary left lateral incisor, already restored with a metal-ceramic crown (FDI 22). After atraumatic flapless extraction, the osteotomy was initiated on the palatal wall of the socket with a lance bur and a 2.2 mm pilot drill, and completed with a sequence of screw bone expanders instead of rotary drills. Expander position and axis were verified intraoperatively with a periapical radiograph and a CBCT scan before the osteotomy was finalized. An implant (“Newton”, Kalodon, 4.25 × 13 mm) was placed in a palatally shifted position with apical bone expansion of the nasal-floor cortex (part of the “supramaxillary arch buttress”, a nomenclature we have proposed), achieving an insertion torque exceeding 60 Ncm. The residual buccal gap was filled with a deproteinized bovine bone mineral xenograft to compensate for the expected resorption of the bundle bone, and a screw-retained provisional restoration was delivered the same day. Healing was uneventful. At three months the peri-implant mucosa was stable and well contoured, with no visible collapse of the buccal contour; the site was digitally scanned and a definitive screw-retained zirconia crown was delivered. Radiographically, the marginal bone level appeared stable at all controls. The patient was then followed for 12 months after crown delivery, with an uneventful course. Conclusions. In a narrow lateral incisor socket, combining “apical expansion” with immediate implant placement, buccal gap grafting and immediate provisionalization allowed a single-surgery, three-month rehabilitation with preserved mucosal architecture. Intraoperative three-dimensional verification of the expander before finalizing the osteotomy was decisive in confirming the implant axis in a site with minimal (bundle) buccal bone. The result was obtained in a heavy smoker with a history of severe periodontitis and should be confirmed with quantitative, longer-term data. Engaging the “supramaxillary arch buttress” of the splanchnocranium ensures the necessary stability.

title: Esophageal Injury During Transesophageal Echocardiography-Guided Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion: A Narrative Review
abstract: Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) remains an established imaging modality for guiding percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO), providing real-time visualization during transseptal puncture, device deployment and procedural assessment. However, esophageal instrumentation and prolonged probe manipulation may result in gastrointestinal injury, particularly in patients with pre-existing esophageal abnormalities or increased bleeding risk. This narrative review summarizes the available evidence regarding the mechanisms, risk factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, management and prevention of TEE-associated esophageal injury during LAAO while examining alternative imaging strategies. A literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library, supplemented by targeted searches of broader structural heart intervention literature. Although clinically recognized TEE-associated gastrointestinal complications are uncommon, studies employing systematic endoscopic surveillance have identified substantially higher rates of subclinical mucosal injury. Reported manifestations range from transient dysphagia and superficial mucosal lesions to gastrointestinal bleeding, intramural esophageal hematoma, perforation and fistula formation. Nevertheless, limited LAAO-specific evidence, heterogeneous outcome definitions and differences in surveillance strategies preclude reliable estimation of procedure-specific esophageal injury incidence. Intracardiac echocardiography eliminates esophageal instrumentation but carries a distinct procedural risk profile, whereas cardiac computed tomography (CCT) provides complementary opportunities for preprocedural planning and postprocedural surveillance. Careful preprocedural assessment, judicious probe manipulation, early recognition of complications and individualized imaging selection are important considerations. Prospective studies incorporating standardized esophageal injury endpoints are needed to establish the true clinical burden and guide preventive strategies.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Medical Image Analysis in Low-Resource Settings
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) for medical image analysis is increasingly being developed for low-resource settings, where specialist expertise, imaging equipment, labelled data, and computing resources may be limited. We systematically reviewed 189 studies published between January 2021 and January 2026 to examine how these constraints relate to imaging modalities, clinical applications, and AI methods in low-resource settings. Each study was also assessed against 15 criteria adapted from the FUTURE-AI principles for trustworthy AI. Shortages of clinical expertise were the most common constraint, and portable or lower-cost imaging was widely used. Transfer learning was the most frequent technical strategy (59%), followed by data augmentation (54%) and efficient model design (36%). Medical-image pretraining and self-supervised learning were each used in 4% of studies, and model compression in 3%. Applications were concentrated in retinal disease, pulmonary disease, antenatal care, parasitic diseases, and cervical screening. Beyond these technical and clinical patterns, the trustworthy AI assessment showed a clear gap between documenting how systems were developed and demonstrating how they performed under relevant local conditions. Subgroup performance was evaluated in 24% of studies, intended users or realistic working conditions in 25%, and model explanations with intended users in 4%. Consistent with this gap, among 15 studies that reported the same model and metric during development and in the local setting, 12 performed worse locally. Future research should prioritise representative local evaluation, intended-user assessment, demonstrated resource suitability, and reproducible research practices.

title: Most Colon Grading Mistakes Are Neighbors: Adjacent-Grade Error Shares and Grade-3 Recall on Public Histopathology Embeddings
abstract: Colon histology computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) papers often lead with pooled grading accuracy. That number mixes easy majority-class hits with minority-class misses and treats a Grade 1↔Grade 2 swap as interchangeable with calling poorly differentiated cancer well differentiated. This preprint recomputes stratified five-fold support-vector grading on 560 public colorectal cancer patches with frozen ResNet50 embeddings (Grade 1 n=251, Grade 2 n=210, Grade 3 n=99). Cross-validated accuracy is 73.6% ± 2.9% and macro-F1 is 0.705, but Grade 3 recall is only 0.475. Of 148 residual mistakes, 119 (80.4%) are adjacent-grade swaps; 29 (19.6%) jump from Grade 3 to Grade 1. A published soft-voting ensemble confusion matrix shows the same structure: 86.0% of errors remain adjacent. We treat that adjacent share as the checkable claim—not a new leaderboard—and argue that Grade 3 recall and adjacent versus non-adjacent error counts should be reported before pooled accuracy is read as a deployment summary. Embedding protocol and ensemble confusion-matrix anchors follow a published two-stage colon pipeline; no new patients were enrolled.

title: Synergistic Therapeutic Effects of Non-Invasive Aesthetic Technologies and Applied Sports Activity in the Management of Localized Adiposity and Cellulite
abstract: Non-invasive aesthetic technologies, such as cryolipolysis (CLL), radiofrequency (RF), and ultrasound cavitation, have become standard therapeutic approaches for the management of localized adiposity and gynoid lipodystrophy (cellulite). While these technologies effectively induce adipocyte apoptosis or lipolysis, the subsequent clearance of cellular debris and free fatty acids (FFAs) heavily relies on the body’s lymphatic and metabolic pathways. This article explores the therapeutic synergy between applied physical activity and non-invasive body contouring. We hypothesize that integrating targeted exercise—specifically aerobic training and targeted muscle contractions—may act as a therapeutic adjunct to aesthetic sections. Physiologically, exercise-induced muscle pumps accelerate lymphatic drainage, facilitating the rapid removal of metabolic byproducts, while increased energy expenditure promotes the oxidation of released FFAs, preventing their re-esterification. By bridging aesthetic science and applied physical activity, this paper proposes a theoretical framework for combined protocols, intended to guide future clinical investigation and offer a holistic, therapeutic approach to body sculpting.

title: A Rare Presentation of Acute-Onset BCG-Induced Aortic Aneurysm: A Case Report
abstract: Background: Mycotic Aortic aneurysms (MAA) are saccular aneurysms of the infected aortic wall. Mycobacterium, compared with other bacteria, is less likely to cause MAA; most cases follow, but it is a rare, late, systemic, and serious complication of intravesical Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) instillation for bladder cancer. Case Presentation: A 65-year-old male with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, diabetic foot ulcer with methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) bacteremia, status post partial toe amputation, and papillary urothelial carcinoma treated with transurethral resection and intravesical BCG instillation, recently underwent a computed tomography (CT) abdomen 2 weeks ago for abdominal pain, which revealed colonic stool without other pathological findings, who currently presented with worsening abdominal pain, and the CT scan identified a new 2.5-centimeter pseudoaneurysm of the infrarenal aorta, associated with a periaortic and aortocaval mass, likely a hematoma, infectious mycotic aneurysm, or neoplastic process. The patient received intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam for presumed MSSA, a potential cause of a mycotic aneurysm, which was later discontinued after negative blood cultures. Vascular surgery consultation led to endovascular aortic stenting. Infectious disease recommended a Karius test; despite no warning signs, it returned positive for the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, and a diagnosis of a BCG-induced aneurysm was made. The patient was treated with isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyridoxine, then continued isoniazid and rifampin for 9 months. Conclusion: We presented a rare case of a BCG-induced mycotic aortic aneurysm that developed within 2 weeks. Therefore, we need a low threshold for MAA in patients with a history of intravesical BCG instillations who present with worsening abdominal pain, even if prior imaging 2 weeks ago showed no warning signs and instillations were given 2 years ago. Testing and diagnosing a BCG-induced aneurysm are necessary despite endovascular intervention, because it can further infect the stent and form an abscess if untreated.

title: Pulmonary Alveolar Microlithiasis: From Clinicopathologic Description to Molecular Pathogenesis and Emerging Therapies
abstract: Pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis (PAM) is a rare autosomal recessive lung disease in which calcium phosphate microliths fill the alveoli. Although the cause of it remained unknown for some time, more recently loss-of-function variants in SLC34A2, which encodes the sodium-phosphate cotransporter NPT2b, explain nearly all genetically tested cases; failure to clear phosphate from the alveolar lining fluid leads to microlith formation, and an epithelial Npt2b-knockout mouse reproduces the human phenotype. Diagnosis now rests mainly on characteristic high-resolution CT and, increasingly, on genotyping rather than lung biopsy. The protracted course has been described in some series of cases, with death from respiratory failure. No drug has proven efficacy; lung transplantation is the only established therapy, and no allograft recurrence has been documented. Preclinical data support phosphate restriction, EDTA lavage and gene-directed approaches. However, controlled trials with more genotype-phenotype correlation and prospective natural-history data are still needed.

title: Gastric Fungal Colonization as a Candidate Mechanism in ALS-Spectrum Motor Neuron Disease: A Hypothesis Supported by Five Years of Case Documentation
abstract: Background: The etiology of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) remains unknown in approximately 90% of cases [1]. A unified mechanism linking environmental mycotoxin exposure, gut-brain axis dysfunction, and motor neuron disease has not been systematically investigated. Hypothesis. Chronic colonization of the gastric mucosa by a mycotoxin-producing mold, concealed beneath a mucosal biofilm and therefore potentially undetectable by standard endoscopy, is proposed to drive sustained motor-neuron hyperexcitability through three concurrent mechanisms: (1) TLR activation on vagal afferent fibers projecting excitatory signals to brainstem motor nuclei via neural spill-over; (2) cross-reactive immune attack on motor-neuron surface proteins via molecular mimicry; and (3) Dectin-1-mediated neuroinflammation during biofilm disruption. Case. Five-year index case: five positive urinary Trichothecene assays including one after a 32-hour fast (internal source confirmed); six immunological assessments, including five CD25 measurements, showing markedly reduced measured T-cell activation markers and cytokine responses (CD25 1.0–3.1%, reference 13–24%; IFN-γ 79.5 pg/ml, reference ≥118; IL-17 5.4 pg/ml, reference ≥9.6); EMG-confirmed neurogenic remodeling followed by documented stabilization; over 30 reproducible pharmacological observations consistent with the proposed mechanism; and formal diagnostic exclusion across four institutions over three years. Implications. Convergent findings from the published literature, together with more than 30 internally consistent pharmacological observations, support formal investigation of the proposed model. Proposed initial investigations include urinary mycotoxin testing, lymphocyte transformation testing, mycotoxin antibody testing, visual contrast sensitivity screening, and biofilm-directed endoscopy with confocal laser endomicroscopy, targeted biopsy, and PCR analysis.

title: Biologically Inspired Selective Attention for Prostate MRI: A Segmentation-Guided Vision Transformer Framework for Computer-Aided Diagnosis
abstract: Prostate cancer is the second most commonly diagnosed malignancy in men, yet interpretation of multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) suffers from substantial inter-observer variability and depends on scarce expert radiologists. Expert readers follow a hierarchical, coarse-to-fine visual strategy: they first localize the prostate gland and then direct focused attention to tissue within it. Inspired by this biological selective-attention mechanism, we propose a segmentation-guided framework in which a modality-aware 3D Vision Transformer (ViT) first delineates the prostate gland from T2-weighted, ADC, and DWI volumes, and the resulting anatomical mask then constrains downstream cancer detection. Global self-attention models long-range anatomical context, analogous to the integration of peripheral and foveal information in human vision. Detection was evaluated through two pathways: gray-level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM) texture features with classical classifiers, and a ViT classifier. On 200 patients from the public PROSTATEx cohort, the proposed segmentation model achieved a Dice similarity coefficient of [0.905] versus [0.831] for an optimized U-Net. The segmentation-guided ViT achieved an AUC of [0.987] and an accuracy of [0.998] for clinically significant cancer detection. Ablation experiments confirmed that anatomical guidance improved both pathways. These results show that emulating expert visual search strategies yields accurate and interpretable computer-aided prostate cancer diagnosis.

title: DeepSUM-DWI: A Joint Image Registration and Super-Resolution Convolutional Neural Network for Diffusion-Weighted MRI
abstract: Background: Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is an important MRI technique for studying tissue microstructure and structural connectivity, but is limited by relatively low spatial resolution, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and sensitivity to inter-acquisition motion. A deep-learning framework was developed that jointly performs image registration and super-resolution on repeated low-resolution DWI inputs to generate a single registered, higher apparent spatial-resolution output. Methods: DeepSUM-DWI adapts a DeepSUM multi-image super-resolution architecture for repeated DWI. It comprises a shared 2D super-resolution feature extractor (SISRNet), a registration network (RegNet), and a 3D fusion network (FusionNet). Evaluation used (1) simulated repetitions with synthetic motion, (2) retrospectively downsampled acquisitions from 12 subjects, and (3) a prospective dual-resolution example with matched 1.0 × 1.0 and 2.0 × 2.0 mm² acquisitions. Results: DeepSUM-DWI reconstructed a single high-resolution-appearing DWI image from multiple low-resolution repetitions while preserving structural characteristics of the high-resolution acquisitions. The model remained robust across synthetic motion magnitudes. In retrospectively downsampled data, it improved NRMSE by 71–79% and PSNR by 10.6–13.5 dB, for super-resolution factors of 2–3, relative to averaging interpolated low-resolution images, with a mean SSIM > 0.99. In prospectively acquired data, it recovered finer structures than visible in the acquired low-resolution images while maintaining contrast consistency. Exploratory diffusion analysis suggested that some gains in apparent detail propagated to FA maps. Conclusions: DeepSUM-DWI provides a framework for joint registration and super-resolution of repeated DWI acquisitions, with potential to improve apparent spatial resolution while retaining the SNR benefits of repeated acquisition.
